observation: The numeral has a separate short horizontal stroke beneath 1, not extending under the raised circle. It may be an underline or the numeral's separate base stroke; both are retained. The closing parenthesis is independent.

The left context supports d' with a detached apostrophe. The cancelled rounded initial body and tall t-like stroke favor autres, but the strike masks the medial joins. The following flattened letters are read as anciens; no additional earlier word is invented.

A long independent strike crosses the complete phrase. Avant and de are readable. The tall/open first body of the last word does not securely distinguish l from c under the strike; les is preferred, ces remains possible.

There are two baselines: a crossed lower word and a live raised replacement. The lower g descender and tall f support signifierait; the raised p/l bodies and long q descender support impliquerait. The compressed medial e/r strokes are not fully separable, so the shorter -iait/-iquait alternatives remain local doubts.

The first body has the p descender, long l ascent and low us sequence of plus. The next two compact groups have flattened rounded strokes; the preferred un cas and alternative en un remain uncertain. No punctuation is supplied.

An accent mark is separately present above the first vowel, and the i point is clear. The final tall l ends in a short low return; I cannot decide whether that return is an additional s. The singular-looking ending is preferred without grammatical normalization.

The mathematical group is heavily retraced and crossed. Triangular segments and a lowered x-like group support Delta_x; the upper horizontal stroke may be an overbar or part of the overwork/cancellation. A lower independent stroke crosses the group. No earlier glyph is inferred from the surviving internal strokes.

The entire expression is read. The left triangle is heavily retraced with an interior upright and a long horizontal stroke crossing its apex. The horizontal stroke supports a barred reading, but it may be a remnant of the overwork; no previous letter is invented. The right T has only its own long roof and separate stem, not an additional overbar. Superscript I(x) has the capital I's upper and lower caps, parentheses and the small x.

The raised L has an independent horizontal bar. The main pi-like sign has one roof and two legs with curved feet. Between the lower L and K the separator is almost upright; a vertical bar is the literal preferred shape, with a steep slash retained as an alternative. The following comma is separate.
The initial long p descender is clear. The middle is flattened and the last tall angled body has no securely separate crossbar. Peut is preferred over par, but the compact word is not fully resolved.
The initial tall h stroke reaches the upper crop edge, but its lower hump and the rest of the word are visible. The separate arch above a supports hâtives; no terminal point is visible.

The lower tail of the section sign and the top of the 2 meet the crop boundaries. The section-sign loop, the oblique 2 with its basal return, and the separate following point remain identifiable; no additional numeral is supplied.

The insertion itself reads cas followed by 2 and a raised circle. The small clipped diagonal at the lower-right edge belongs to adjacent ink and is not completed as an additional character or parenthesis.
The lower margin number is 130 in thinner strokes. The dark border beneath it is the page edge, not a written underline.

The left body is a single compressed cup-and-arch sequence, compatible with un or en. It is not confidently reduced to a punctuation dash. The separate upright stroke and lower dot on the right form an exclamation mark.
